title: Chandelier Cells
intro: Chandelier cells, also called axo-axonic cells, are the most target-specific neurons known. Every one of their output synapses lands on the axon initial segment of a pyramidal cell, the exact spot where action potentials start, in short vertical rows of boutons that look like candles on a chandelier. A single chandelier cell contacts hundreds of pyramidal cells, and each pyramidal cell receives input from a few chandelier cells.

items: Morphology: discovered by Szentagothai and Arbib (1974) and Somogyi (1977). The axon ends in 'cartridges', vertical strings of boutons, each wrapped around one axon initial segment. Somata mostly sit at the layer 1/2 border and in layer 6 of cortex, and in the pyramidal layer of hippocampus.

Molecular identity: part of the PV family (many but not all express parvalbumin), born late in development from the medial ganglionic eminence; a specific transcriptomic type ('Pvalb Vipr2' in Allen nomenclature).
Firing: fast spiking, similar to basket cells.

Connectivity: one chandelier cell innervates up to a few hundred pyramidal cells, contacting a large fraction (about 35 to 50 per cent in mouse, Inan et al. 2013) of the pyramidal cells within its axonal field; they receive input from local pyramidal cells and long-range sources.

Inhibitory or excitatory? Because the chloride gradient in the axon initial segment can be depolarising, Szabadics et al. (2006) found chandelier cells could excite pyramidal cells in cortical slices. Later work (Woodruff et al. 2011) suggested they are mostly inhibitory at physiological potentials, and in vivo optogenetic studies in adult mice find mainly inhibitory effects (Lu et al. 2017). The question is not fully closed, and the effect may depend on the state of the target.

blocks.text: Synapses on the axon initial segment act as a veto on spike generation, so chandelier cells are often described as gatekeepers of pyramidal output: they could silence a whole population at once, synchronise its output, or reset it. Their density and their links to epilepsy and schizophrenia (Lewis et al. 2005 reported reduced GABA transporter at chandelier cartridges in schizophrenia) suggest an important role, but which computation they serve in normal function is still open. Schneider-Mizell et al. (2021) combined electron microscopy of chandelier synapses in mouse visual cortex with in vivo imaging and found that chandelier cells are strongly activated with arousal and locomotion, and that the number of chandelier synapses varies widely between target cells.

items: Detailed: Blue Brain's ChC m-type in each layer, with cNAC (continuous non-accommodating) fast-spiking e-types.
Point neurons: the same fast-spiking model as basket cells (Izhikevich FS, Wang-Buzsaki).

Synapse placement: the defining feature, inhibition at the axon initial segment, can only be represented in a model with an axon compartment. In a point-neuron model it becomes strong shunting or veto inhibition on the spike mechanism, for example inhibition that briefly raises threshold or clamps the membrane.
Studies of their excitatory versus inhibitory action use compartmental models of the axon initial segment with chloride dynamics (e.g. Woodruff et al. 2011).

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Most column models leave chandelier cells out, and for a first model that is reasonable.
If you need a population-level 'veto' or reset of output, a chandelier-like population that strongly shunts many pyramidal cells at once is the biological precedent.
Keep them distinct from basket cells if you study output gating: basket cells shape timing, chandelier cells can block output at the source.
